fullName: Atomic: a beamline for extremely high-resolution coherent imaging of atomistic structures (Bragg coherent diffraction imaging, 34-ID-F)

status2026.detail: On the APS 'Beamline Commissioning Progress' chart dated 2026-10-05, '34-ID-F: ATOMIC XSD' sits at stage 5 of 6 ('Scientific Commissioning and Early Experiments'), not yet stage 6 ('Restart of General User Program'). The APS Proposal Types page (dated 2026-10-07) already lists 34-ID-F among beamlines taking General User and Rapid Access proposals, so general-user operation is expected to follow. History: a Dec 2021 user town hall covered the timing and scope of 34-ID construction; the Dec 2023 plan was scientific commissioning in cycle 2025-1; Dec 2024/Jan 2025 updates said only 'infrastructure' for Atomic/3DMN would be in place when the project closed in mid-2025; Aug 2025 update expected first light in October 2025 and first users late in run 2026-1; the Oct 2025 update reported Atomic moved into commissioning ('all of the feature beamlines are now online'); the 2026-01-26 chart showed stage 4, technical commissioning. MEDSI 2025 states all nine feature beamlines met their Key Performance Parameters. Stale pages: the Beamline Directory status field still reads 'Construction' and the Feature Beamlines page still says 'Atomic (to come)'. No peer-reviewed post-upgrade ATOMIC result was found as of 2026-10-09; 2026 science highlights crediting '34-ID-C' appear to report pre-upgrade data. Project context: the January 2026 update said the upgrade had 'all scope delivered', and the APS-U project received final approval (CD-4) in January 2026; the MEDSI 2025 KPPs were brightness at a defined energy plus verification of the usable energy range (only ISN had a spot-size KPP), so meeting them does not demonstrate the 50 nm zoom spot.

tagline: A lens-free X-ray microscope that rebuilds single nanocrystals in 3D and reveals the strain hidden inside them.
summary: ATOMIC, at the far end of beamline 34-ID, makes 3D images of the inside of single crystals smaller than a bacterium, such as specks of battery material, catalyst or metal. Instead of a lens it uses Bragg coherent diffractive imaging (BCDI): a coherent X-ray beam, whose waves march in step, strikes a crystal at exactly the angle at which its layers of atoms reflect, and a camera records the speckled pattern that bounces off. Rocking the crystal through a fraction of a degree builds that pattern up in 3D; a computer then works backwards to the crystal's shape and to where its atomic layers are pushed or pulled out of place, the strain and defects that help decide whether a battery lasts or a metal cracks. Bendable 'zoom' mirrors are designed to size the spot to each crystal, from 2 µm down to 50 nm. In October 2026 ATOMIC is in scientific commissioning.

whatAPSUEnables.text: Coherent imaging can use only the part of an X-ray beam whose waves march in step: on the old APS, about 0.04% of the light at an X-ray energy of 10 keV. In the design's brightness mode the upgraded ring's electron beam is about 19 times narrower horizontally (14.7 µm root-mean-square width instead of 280 µm) and three times narrower vertically, raising that share to an estimated 5%. Slits and zoom mirrors put this core on each crystal: by design, 3.1 × 10¹² photons per second in a 0.1% energy band reach a 50 nm spot at 8.7 keV. The design expects 3D images of crystals in working devices, finer than 10 nm, in tens of seconds, not minutes, though heating, radiation damage and about 400 times more data become design problems. The headline gain, about 540 times more coherent flux at 20 keV, assumes an undulator optimized for 20 keV; at ATOMIC's ~9 keV it is smaller, and nothing measured is published yet.
quantitative: Time per 3D BCDI data set: several minutes at third-generation sources (about 2 min per operando 3D scan at 34-ID-C) vs sub-10-nm operando imaging expected in tens of seconds at APS-U (PDR estimate).

Coherent flux at 20 keV: 3.12 × 10¹³ ph/s (APS-U brightness mode) vs 6 × 10¹⁰ ph/s (pre-upgrade APS), a factor of ~520; the FDR quotes 'a factor of 540 at 20 keV'. These Table 1.1 values are for an undulator optimized for 20 keV, not ATOMIC's 2.1 m revolver; at ATOMIC's ~9 keV the gain is smaller (derived: coherent-fraction gain ~125× at 10 keV, times ~2–3× more central-cone flux).
Horizontal source size 14.7 µm rms vs 280 µm rms before the upgrade (19× smaller); horizontal divergence 2.8 vs 11.6 µrad.

Coherent fraction at 10 keV, brightness mode, 2.1 m undulator: ~5% (f_{x} ≈ 0.11, f_{y} ≈ 0.48) vs ~0.04% before the upgrade, derived here from the FDR Table 1.1 source parameters with σ_{r} = √(2λL)/4π and σ′_{r} = √(λ/2L).
Flux into the focus at 8.7 keV: 3.1 × 10¹² ph/s/0.1%BW in 50 nm and 4.6 × 10¹² in 2 µm (brightness mode); 1.8 × 10¹² and 2.5 × 10¹² in timing mode (FDR Table 4.65).
Focal spot range 50 nm – 2 µm (simulated 47 × 50 nm² to 2.1 × 2.1 µm² at 8.7 keV) vs ~0.5 × 0.7 µm (H × V) typical at pre-upgrade 34-ID-C: ~140× smaller spot area at the small end.
Estimated time for 3D atomic-resolution CDI of a 50 nm volume: ~1,000 s at 4.9 × 10¹² ph/s into 50 nm (PDR estimate, based on Dietze & Shpyrko's ~10¹⁸ ph/µm² requirement for a 20 nm Au crystal).
Data: ~0.65 TB a year at 34-ID-C vs 250–300 TB a year expected at ATOMIC (~400×).
Resolution target ≤ 1 nm (FDR) vs 10–30 nm 3D resolution and ~2 × 10⁻⁴ strain resolution typical of BCDI at third-generation sources.

techniques.name: Bragg coherent diffractive imaging
techniques.text: Bragg coherent diffractive imaging (BCDI) lights an isolated crystal, tens of nanometres to about 2 µm across, with a coherent beam at its Bragg angle, the angle at which one family of its atomic planes reflects. The reflected X-rays interfere into a 3D speckle pattern, recorded slice by slice as the crystal is rocked through a fraction of a degree (76 one-second frames over ±0.3° in one 34-ID-C study). The detector records only intensities; iterative algorithms recover the missing phases, provided each speckle spans at least two pixels in every direction. The result shows the crystal's shape and how far its atoms are displaced perpendicular to the reflecting planes, to a fraction of an ångström (0.1 nm), and strain (fractional stretch) to about 10⁻⁴. Pre-upgrade 3D resolution was typically 10–30 nm; ATOMIC aims for 1 nm or better.

techniques.name: Laue-assisted multi-reflection BCDI (full strain tensor)
techniques.text: One reflection shows atomic displacement along a single direction; the full strain tensor, all six components of stretch and shear, needs at least three reflections whose directions do not lie in one plane. Finding them on a crystal of unknown orientation is the hard part. So the crystal is first lit with the pink beam, many energies at once, which gives many reflections together in a Laue pattern; software (LaueGo) indexes its spots, assigning each to a set of atomic planes, which gives the crystal's exact orientation. The monochromator then moves in for Bragg coherent imaging at three or more reflections, its heated second crystal keeping the single-energy beam on the pink beam's path through the focusing mirrors.

techniques.name: Bragg ptychography (scanning BCDI)
techniques.text: For crystals or films larger than the biggest zoom spot, about 1.5–2 µm, the beam is stepped across the sample in overlapping positions and a speckle pattern is recorded at each. The overlap does more than stitch a panorama: the shared regions give the computer enough redundancy to recover both the sample and the exact shape of the probing beam, so strain can be imaged over a larger area. The zoom mirrors let the spot size be traded against the number of scan positions. The mode is planned but not yet documented as commissioned at 34-ID-F.

techniques.name: Atomic-resolution (wide-angle) coherent diffractive imaging
techniques.text: The long-term goal behind the beamline's name is to see individual atoms in 3D, in crystals and in non-crystalline samples. The finest detail lies in faint speckle far from the main reflection, out to a scattering vector (a measure of scattering angle) of about 1 Å⁻¹, which matches the spacing between atoms; out there the intensity has fallen roughly as the inverse fourth power of the distance from the reflection. Recording it takes a huge dose: by Dietze and Shpyrko's estimate, about 10¹⁸ photons per µm² for a crystalline gold particle and ten times less for an amorphous one. A design-report example, a metallic-glass nanopillar, would need about an hour for a 10-view tomographic set. The goal is aspirational and not yet demonstrated at ATOMIC.

techniques.name: Polychromatic / pink-beam coherent imaging
techniques.text: A wider band of X-ray energies, the pink beam, carries many more photons than a single-energy beam, which helps with weakly scattering samples and with fast imaging. The 2019 Final Design Report defines a 'Pink Beam CDI' (coherent diffractive imaging) mode that delivers focused pink beam to the endstation; mirrors focus all energies alike, so the zoom optics accept the full energy width of an undulator peak (harmonic). The 2017 design anticipated reconstruction methods that handle many energies or several coherent modes at once, and broadband 3D imaging without rotating the sample. Whether the mode is in use at 34-ID-F is not known.

techniques.name: Operando / in situ BCDI with AI-accelerated phase retrieval
techniques.text: Crystals are imaged inside working devices: a coin-cell battery under charge, a gas-flow heater up to 900 °C, a cryo chamber near 80 K or a liquid-flow cell, all fitting in the ~50 mm between the last mirror and its focus. Argonne's cohere package runs the slow iterative phase retrieval on graphics processors (GPUs) and pairs it with neural networks. Once trained, AutoPhaseNN reconstructs about 100 times faster than iterative methods (more than 10 times, by Argonne's 2024 computing strategy) and supplies their starting guess; the physics-aware 3D-CDI-NN predicts structure and strain hundreds of times faster, quick enough to steer an experiment as it runs. The 2017 design also planned element-specific (resonant) and polarization-sensitive (dichroic) coherent imaging with a diamond phase plate; the final design dropped it.

scienceCases.title: Watching batteries break (and heal) from the inside
scienceCases.text: Battery electrodes are made of tiny crystals that swell and shrink every time the battery charges, and the defects inside them help decide how fast it wears out. Bragg coherent imaging at the APS watched dislocations (line defects in the stacking of atoms) appear, move and vanish in nanoparticles of a lithium–nickel–manganese oxide cathode inside a working cell (Ulvestad and colleagues, Science 2015). Later work, much of it at 34-ID-C, found metastable dislocation loops in sodium-ion cathodes, defects in a solid electrolyte and a phase-transformation front crossing a cathode particle at about 2 minutes per 3D scan. ATOMIC's coherent flux and 50 nm zoom spot target images of working cells finer than 10 nm in tens of seconds.

scienceCases.title: Seeing where catalysts work
scienceCases.text: Catalyst particles speed up chemical reactions mostly at their corners and edges. Bragg coherent diffractive imaging (BCDI) of gold crystals about 300 nm across, during the breakdown of ascorbic acid, showed strain concentrating at the corners; reactive molecular-dynamics simulations traced it to hydroxyl groups bound to the surface (Ulvestad and colleagues, 2016). The 2017 design report's flagship experiment would image a silver–gold alloy nanocrystal while it is electrochemically dealloyed, using anomalous coherent diffractive imaging: tuning the X-ray energy to about 12 keV, gold's L₃ absorption edge, where gold's scattering changes sharply and so singles out the gold. It would then follow catalysis and coarsening in the nanoporous gold left behind, repeating it on crystals of different sizes with the zoom optics.

scienceCases.title: Defects in tough metals for fusion and aerospace
scienceCases.text: Strong metals are full of microscopic flaws that affect how a part survives heat and radiation. Hofmann and colleagues (2020) located specific dislocations, line defects in the stacking of atoms, in tungsten with Laue microdiffraction at 34-ID-E, cut micro-crystals around them with a focused ion beam (FIB), and imaged the full strain tensor, stretch and shear in every direction, by Bragg coherent diffractive imaging (BCDI) at 34-ID-C. Related studies at 10–30 nm resolution followed FIB damage annealing out of gold and a cobalt–iron crystal corroding. At the APS, a dislocation loop was also seen being absorbed into a grain boundary in a gold film heated to about 400 °C (Yau and colleagues, Science 2017). ATOMIC adds in situ Laue orientation and a beam sized to grains embedded in films.

scienceCases.title: How crystals grow: clues frozen in strain
scienceCases.text: When minerals grow from water, impurities and the path of growth leave strain locked inside each crystal. Bragg coherent diffractive imaging (BCDI) at 34-ID-C followed calcite and barite growing with and without strontium ions. Calcite kept a high density of defects and preserved lattice strain, consistent with nonclassical growth from prenucleation clusters or amorphous (disordered) precursors, while barite grew in the classical way, ion by ion. High-resolution electron microscopy and molecular-dynamics simulations backed the reading (Yuan and colleagues, JACS 2026).

scienceCases.title: Atom-by-atom failure in metallic glass (aspirational)
scienceCases.text: Metallic glasses are very strong metals whose atoms have no crystalline order, and they fail suddenly. The dream is to image the atoms rearranging just before a tiny glass pillar yields. A feasibility study in the 2017 design report modelled a 20 nm Cu₆₄Zr₃₆ pillar of 96,000 atoms: patterns recorded far out from the centre, to 1.26 Å⁻¹, would locate its atoms to 0.1 Å. With about 2 × 10¹² photons per second (in a 0.01% energy band) focused into 20 × 26 nm², each data set would take about 7 minutes, and each strain state, seen from some 10 orientations, about an hour. Amorphous samples like this need about ten times less dose than crystals for atomic resolution (Dietze and Shpyrko).

scienceCases.title: Spin-lattice coupling in quantum materials (planned)
scienceCases.text: In some exotic oxides, magnetism and the crystal lattice are tightly linked. The 2017 design report proposed resonant Bragg coherent diffractive imaging (BCDI), with the X-ray energy tuned to an element's absorption edge, to image the antiferromagnetic twin domains of the iridate Sr₂IrO₄, a material whose neighbouring magnetic moments point in opposite directions, across temperature and magnetic field. A diamond phase plate would control the polarization (circular up to about 12 keV) and allow dichroic BCDI, which compares opposite polarizations, of magnetic materials. Such images could show how defects disturb the magnetic patterns. The final design does not list a phase plate, so this remains a future option.

scienceCases.title: Imaging at the speed of the experiment
scienceCases.text: ATOMIC is expected to write 250–300 terabytes (TB) of data a year, about 400 times more than 34-ID-C's ~0.65 TB; fast Bragg coherent imaging alone writes about 20 megabytes per second. Argonne is speeding up reconstruction to match. Its cohere package spreads phase retrieval over many graphics processors (GPUs), and neural networks (AutoPhaseNN, and the physics-aware 3D-CDI-NN refined by automatic differentiation) turn speckle into 3D images far faster than iterative methods, so scientists can decide what to measure next while the experiment runs. AI also aligns the nanofocusing mirrors: AutoFocus was developed on a digital twin of the bendable Kirkpatrick–Baez (KB) mirrors at 34-ID-C and validated on a similar system at 28-ID-B.

insertionDevices.name: ATOMIC revolver undulator – 21 mm array (APS21R25#8S, magnet structure APS21#13S)
insertionDevices.type: planar hybrid permanent-magnet revolver undulator (two magnet structures on a rotating strongback, common 4-motor gap separation mechanism)
insertionDevices.notes: Downstream device of the 34-ID straight → inboard canted beam (FDR Table 4.62). As installed: 98 periods, device minimum gap 8.5 mm, K_eff 1.38, E1 = 8.33 keV at minimum gap (tunable up to ~16 keV as K → 0), total power 4.8 kW, peak 190 kW/mrad² at 200 mA. The 3rd harmonic covers ~25 keV and above for the 30 keV end of the range (derived). FDR maximum power through the 2 × 2 mm² mask at 30 m: 763/738 W for the two arrays (pairing of values to arrays ambiguous in FDR Table 4.62). The ID table marks it as a short device; the Beamline Directory quotes 2.3 m (likely the overall length). ID-table gap limits for S34 DS: device minimum 8.5 mm, administrative minimum 8.65 mm, user minimum 9.0 mm. The tabulated K and E1 are at 8.5 mm, so at the 9.0 mm user minimum E1 is slightly higher (~8.9–9.1 keV for U21, ~5.0–5.1 keV for U25, derived from Halbach-type hybrid field scaling; consistent with the 5.3 keV lower limit).

insertionDevices.name: ATOMIC revolver undulator – 25 mm array (same device, APS25#10S)
insertionDevices.type: planar hybrid permanent-magnet revolver undulator (alternate magnet structure)
insertionDevices.notes: Same physical device as above; only one array is active at a time (rotated with the gap open). 82 periods, K_eff 1.99, E1 = 4.59 keV at minimum gap, total power 7.0 kW, 196 kW/mrad². Provides the low end of the 5.3–30 keV range. FDR revolver description: Sec. 3-3.3.2.

source.canting: Two undulators canted by 1.0 mrad in the 34-ID straight, using electromagnetic canting magnets of 0.5 / 1.0 / 0.5 mrad (upstream / centre / downstream) plus a corrector in the middle (FDR Ch. 3 Table 3.20 and ID configuration table). ATOMIC uses the downstream revolver and the inboard beam, 3DMN the upstream U28 and the outboard beam. At the 25.4 m exit mask the two 2 × 2 mm² apertures are ~25 mm apart (1 mrad × 25.4 m, derived). Before the upgrade the coherent-imaging station 34-ID-C used the outboard beam from the upstream undulator and 34-ID-E the inboard beam; the assignment is now reversed.
source.frontEnd: Canted Undulator Front End (CUFE) rated 2 × 10 kW total and 280 kW/mrad² peak power density, with a windowless (differential-pump) exit for 34-ID. APS-U CUFE features: permanent-magnet clearing magnet upstream of the low-power photon shutter (LPPS), storage-ring valve, burn-through fixed mask 1, fixed masks (the upstream mask at 19.4 m is designed for up to 418 W/mm², an FDR design case for a superconducting-undulator source, not ATOMIC's revolver), GRID fluorescence XBPM1 plus XBPM2 integrated in the exit mask, photon and safety shutters (SS1/SS2). Exit table in 34-ID-A: exit mask at 25.4 m with two 2 × 2 mm² apertures, W exit collimator 2 × (5 × 5 mm²) at 26.1 m.
source.sourceSizeAndDivergence: Electron beam at the ID (FDR Table 1.1): brightness mode (324 bunches, 42 pm) σ_{x} = 14.7 µm, σ_{y} = 3.2 µm, σ′_{x} = 2.8 µrad, σ′_{y} = 1.3 µrad; timing mode (48 bunches, 32 pm) 12.9 / 8.8 µm and 2.5 / 3.7 µrad; pre-upgrade APS 280 / 10.0 µm and 11.6 / 3.4 µrad. Photon source for the 2.1 m revolver at 8.7 keV (derived, Gaussian single-electron terms): Σ_{x} ≈ 14.8 µm, Σ_{y} ≈ 3.8 µm, Σ′_{x} ≈ 6.5 µrad, Σ′_{y} ≈ 6.0 µrad (brightness mode), i.e. coherent fractions ~12% (H) and ~51% (V), ~6% in total. Caveat: the canted source points sit ~1 m from the straight centre, where the beta functions differ slightly from the Table 1.1 values.

U28 (upstream undulator) → shared CUFE and 34-ID-A FOE → outboard flat mirror at 29.6 m → masks in 34-ID-B → HDCM in 34-ID-C (53.8 m) → micro-diffraction station (~60 m) and designed nano-diffraction position (~65.5 m, installation unconfirmed) in 34-ID-E. components.name: U28 planar undulator (upstream device, feeds 3DMN) – partner
components.distanceNote: Upstream device of the same straight, centre ~-1.2 m from the straight centre (approx., as in the 3DMN exhibit).
components.text: The first undulator in this straight section feeds 3DMN, ATOMIC's twin beamline next door, which maps crystal grains in 3D with a many-energy 'rainbow' beam. It is a 2.1 m row of magnets with a 28 mm period, the repeat length of the magnet pattern; at its 8.5 mm minimum gap its lowest-energy peak, the fundamental, lies near 3.0 keV. Its beam leaves 1 milliradian outboard of ATOMIC's. It is shown for context only.

components.name: Canting magnets (1 mrad)
components.distanceNote: Centre magnet at the straight centre (0 m, the distance reference); 0.5 mrad magnets at both ends of the straight (~±2.45 m, approx.). Not tabulated in FDR Sec. 4-9.
components.text: Three small electromagnets, bending by 0.5, 1.0 and 0.5 milliradians, steer the electrons so that the two undulators in this straight section point 1 milliradian, about 0.06°, apart. Their X-ray beams drift apart, about 25 mm by the front-end exit mask, so one slot in the ring feeds two beamlines: ATOMIC, on the downstream undulator and the inboard beam, and its twin 3DMN, on the upstream undulator and the outboard beam.

components.name: Revolver undulator U21/U25 (downstream device, inboard beam)
components.distanceNote: Distances in this exhibit are measured from the centre of the 34-ID straight section (the PDR's definition of 'source'; FDR Table 4.63 lists distances 'from source'). The revolver is the downstream device: its centre sits ~1.2 m downstream of the straight centre (approx., as in the 3DMN exhibit), which may explain ~1 m offsets between the FDR component table/drawings and the FDR ray-trace (see the zoom-KB notes).
components.text: ATOMIC's X-ray source: a 2.1 m row of alternating permanent magnets that steers the ring's electrons into a tight slalom, so they emit an intense, narrow X-ray beam. It is a 'revolver': it carries two magnet arrays, one repeating every 21 mm and one every 25 mm, and with the gap open it rotates 90° to swap them. Closing the gap strengthens the field, lowering the beam's lowest-energy peak, the fundamental: at the 8.5 mm minimum gap it sits at 8.33 keV with the 21 mm array and 4.59 keV with the 25 mm array, and odd harmonics, at 3, 5 … times that energy, reach the top of the 5.3–30 keV range. Users work at gaps of 9.0 mm or more, which shifts each peak slightly higher.

specs.swap: strongbacks rotate 90° with the gap open

components.name: Canted undulator front end (CUFE)
components.distanceNote: 19.4 m is the documented position of the CUFE upstream fixed mask (FDR Ch. 3, XBPM1 power table). The front end runs inside the storage-ring tunnel up to the ratchet wall (~24.4 m), with its exit table in 34-ID-A. Model: a schematic train ~15.6–24.0 m (clearing magnet, LPPS, ring valve, burn-through mask, fixed mask at 19.4 m, XBPM1, photon shutter, two safety shutters, differential pumps) in the FDR Ch. 3 order; positions other than the 19.4 m mask are illustrative. The 418 W/mm² rating of that mask is an FDR design case (SCU source), not an ATOMIC operating value.
components.text: The gatekeeper between accelerator and beamline, inside the tunnel's shielding. This canted-undulator front end (CUFE) carries both beams: its masks soak up kilowatts of unwanted heat (it is rated for two beams of 10 kW each), a beam-position monitor measures where they point, and photon and safety shutters can stop them completely. It has no exit window: differential pumping keeps the vacuums apart, because even a thin window would spoil the coherent beam ATOMIC depends on.

specs.XBPM: GRID XBPM1 + XBPM2 in exit mask
specs.elements: clearing magnet, low-power photon shutter, storage-ring valve, burn-through fixed mask, fixed masks, GRID XBPM1, photon and safety shutters

components.name: Front-end exit mask with XBPM2
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.text: A solid metal block with two 2 mm square openings, one for each of the twin beams, about 25 mm apart. Only the bright central core of each beam passes into the first optics hutch; the rest is absorbed. A second X-ray beam-position monitor (XBPM2) is built into it.

components.name: Front-end exit collimator
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.text: A tungsten block with two 5 mm square openings, one per beam. It stops bremsstrahlung, very-high-energy gamma rays made when stored electrons strike leftover gas in the ring, from following the X-rays into the beamline. Its openings were narrowed for the upgrade to help beamlines like this one, whose monochromators shift the beam sideways by only about 1 mm.

components.name: White-beam slits S1 (inboard, 34ID-SL-1)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63 (PDR: ~27 m).
components.text: Tungsten-edged jaws that trim ATOMIC's beam 26.8 m from the source. They are the first of two coherence-defining apertures (S1): closed down, they act as a small new source, whose light stays in step across the optics downstream; opened, they let through a larger, partially coherent beam with more photons. The second pair, S2, sits 23.5 m downstream.

specs.mode: closed: secondary source; open: partially coherent beam

components.name: Tungsten bremsstrahlung collimator (34ID-BC-1)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.text: A tungsten radiation shield at 28.4 m with clearance holes for both beams. It blocks bremsstrahlung, high-energy gamma rays from the ring that would otherwise follow the X-rays down the line; the lead collimator just behind it catches what gets past.

components.name: Lead bremsstrahlung collimator (34ID-BC-2)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.text: A lead shield right behind the tungsten one, at 28.7 m, with openings for the two beams. Together they catch the stray high-energy radiation around both beam paths before it reaches the mirrors just downstream.

components.name: 3DMN outboard white-beam mirror (34ID-MR-1) – partner
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.text: 3DMN's twin of ATOMIC's mirror bends the neighbouring beam the other way, away from the ring, at the same 3.0 mrad grazing angle. After both mirrors the two beams diverge by about 13 milliradians, enough for each to get its own optics downstream; ATOMIC's beam passes about 30 mm inboard of this mirror. It is shown for context.

components.name: Inboard white-beam mirror (34ID-MR-2)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63 (PDR: 31 m). The 3DMN outboard mirror sits at 29.6 m.
components.text: A flat silicon mirror that the beam strikes at a grazing angle of 3.0 mrad, about 0.17°. It deflects ATOMIC's beam toward the ring, away from its twin, and also acts as a filter: above a critical energy set by its coating, reflectivity falls steeply and the highest X-ray energies, unwanted harmonics, are lost. Three stripes, bare silicon, rhodium and platinum, chosen by moving the mirror up or down, put that cutoff near 10, 22 or 28 keV (estimates). A notch in the substrate limits distortion from the heat it absorbs.

components.name: Secondary bremsstrahlung collimator (34ID-SC-2)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63 (branch not stated; follows the ATOMIC mirror, by analogy with SC-1 after the 3DMN mirror).
components.text: A bremsstrahlung collimator just after ATOMIC's mirror. The mirror turns the X-rays by 6 mrad, but gamma rays from the ring do not reflect: they carry straight on and are caught here, so only the mirror-reflected beam travels downstream.

components.name: Diagnostic flag (34ID-BD-1)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.text: A diagnostic flag: a screen that staff can lower into the beam path, where it glows under the X-rays and shows exactly where the beam is. It sits in the first optics hutch, just downstream of both white-beam mirrors, and is moved out of the way during experiments.

components.name: Pink photon mask / white-beam stop (34ID-PM-1)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.text: The end of the road for unwanted light: a heavy block that absorbs both straight-through 'white' beams, the undulators' full spectrum, and lets only the two mirror-reflected 'pink' beams pass, pink because the mirrors have trimmed off the highest energies. From here on, only these cleaned beams travel downstream.

components.name: Shielded transport 34-ID-A to 34-ID-B (34ID-ST-1)
components.distanceNote: Spans 36.0–42.5 m (FDR Table 4.63; existing white-beam shielded transport reused).
components.text: A lead-shielded pipe that carries both beams safely 6.5 m across open experiment floor, between the first optics hutch (34-ID-A) and the small hutch 34-ID-B. It is the white-beam transport from before the upgrade, reused.

components.name: Inboard pink-beam photon mask (34ID-PM-2)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63 (outboard PM-3 for 3DMN at the same position).
components.text: A metal aperture in hutch 34-ID-B that trims the edges of ATOMIC's pink beam before it reaches the optics hutch. Its counterpart for 3DMN sits at the same distance, 46.9 m, on the outboard beam.

components.name: Lead collimator / bremsstrahlung stop (34ID-BC-3)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.text: A last lead shield with openings for the two beams. It stops any remaining high-energy bremsstrahlung before the optics hutch, so that the hutches downstream, and the people working in them, are protected.

components.name: Beam position monitor (34ID-BD-2)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.text: A beam position monitor in the optics hutch, 34-ID-C, that reports where ATOMIC's beam is. Drifts caught here can be corrected before they move the focused spot off a crystal less than a micrometre across, some 20 m downstream.

components.name: Coherence-defining slits S2 (34ID-SL-3)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63 (PDR: ~51 m).
components.text: A second pair of adjustable jaws (S2), 23.5 m after the first. Light from the small opening of S1 spreads as it travels, and its waves stay in step across a patch that widens with distance; S2 passes just that patch. Together the two apertures select anything from a single coherent mode, a beam whose waves are in step across its whole width, to several modes per direction with more photons, depending on the energy. S2 is also the entrance aperture of the zoom mirrors.

specs.selects: one to several coherent modes per plane, energy-dependent (PDR)

components.name: Horizontal small-offset double-crystal monochromator (34ID-MN-1)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63 (PDR: 51.5 m; FDR Fig. 4.58 drawing shows the chamber at ~51.5–52.2 m, approx).
components.text: A monochromator: two perfect silicon crystals that pass only a narrow band of X-ray energies, chosen anywhere from 5.3 to 30 keV by turning the crystals. Clean speckle needs it: rays scattered from different parts of a crystal must differ in path by less than the beam's coherence length along its direction, about 0.5 µm at 10 keV with these crystals. The crystals shift the beam sideways by only about 1.1 mm and can slide out of the way to let the full pink beam through for Laue orientation pictures; the second crystal is warmed about 60 K above the first, tuning its atomic spacing so that the single-energy beam follows the pink beam's path to the sample.

components.name: 3DMN small-offset DCM (34ID-MN-2) – partner
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63 (3DMN BPM 52.7 m and slits 53.1 m precede it; not drawn).
components.text: 3DMN's own crystal monochromator shares the optics hutch with ATOMIC's, about 0.35 m to the outboard side. 3DMN's signature method uses the full pink beam, so most of the time this monochromator stands aside. It is shown for context.

specs.position: ~0.35 m outboard of the ATOMIC beam

components.name: Zoom KB pair 1 (bendable, 34ID-MR-3)
components.distanceNote: FDR text ('first KB pair... in station C at 54 m'), FDR Fig. 4.58 drawing and PDR Table 6.5 all give ~54 m; FDR Table 4.63 lists 52.0 m; FDR Fig. 4.64 ray-trace source-to-mirror distances are 52.7–53.2 m (probably measured from the undulator rather than the straight centre). This exhibit uses ~54 m in the layout frame.
components.text: The first half of a mirror 'zoom lens'. Kirkpatrick–Baez (KB) mirrors are a crossed pair of curved, grazing-incidence mirrors, one focusing vertically and one horizontally; here both are 350 mm long and bendable. Changing their curvature by micrometres moves the intermediate focus they form anywhere from about 1.3 to 14 m downstream. That focus is the source for the second pair, about 15 m further on: moving it changes how much of the final mirrors is lit, and so the size of the final spot, without moving the focal point at the sample. Each mirror's surface must stay within 1 nm (rms) of its ideal shape while it is bent.

specs.deflection: pair deflects in both planes (H mirror first at ~52.7 m, V mirror at ~53.2 m in the ray-trace frame; deflection senses not documented)

components.name: Pink-beam shutter (inboard, 34ID-SH-1)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63 (3DMN SH-2 at the same position).
components.text: A safety shutter at the downstream wall of the optics hutch, 54.8 m from the source. It closes ATOMIC's beam whenever someone enters ATOMIC's experiment hutch, while 3DMN's beam, with its own shutter at the same position, keeps running.

components.name: Shielded pipe through 34-ID-E (34ID-ST-2)
components.distanceNote: Spans 55.1–67.5 m (FDR Table 4.63); FDR Fig. 4.58 shows it ~0.4 m inboard of the 3DMN beam with periodic supports (approx).
components.text: ATOMIC's beam crosses the whole 3DMN hutch, 34-ID-E, inside this 12.4 m shielded pipe, about 0.4 m from the 3DMN beam. The shielding lets researchers work beside it, and both beamlines run independently.

components.name: 3DMN micro- and nano-diffraction stations (34-ID-E) – partner
components.distanceNote: Micro station ~60.0–60.1 m and nano station ~65.5–65.6 m (FDR Table 4.63 / 3DMN dossier); drawn as ghosted silhouettes.
components.text: ATOMIC's beam runs past 3DMN's two design positions: a micro-diffraction station at about 60 m and a planned nano-diffraction station at about 65.5 m, the latter inside its own temperature-stable enclosure. Whether the nano station is installed is unpublished. Both beamlines can run at the same time. They are drawn as ghosted outlines for context.

components.name: End-station beam pre-conditioning platform (BPM, apodizing apertures)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63 lists 'K-B Mirror (Atomic) 34ID-MR-4' at 68.1 m; PDR places BPM2 at 68 m. Exact contents of the 'End-station Beam Pre-conditioning Platform' (FDR 4-9.9.2) are not published; BPM/apertures here are inferred from the PDR.
components.text: A stable table at the entrance to ATOMIC's hutch, just before the final mirrors. The 2019 Final Design Report lists this 'beam pre-conditioning platform' without detailing it. The 2017 design put a beam position monitor here, and apodizing apertures that remove the faint side lobes a slit edge adds to the beam by diffraction, which would otherwise wash out the speckle fringes.

components.name: Zoom KB pair 2 (final focusing, 34ID-MR-4)
components.distanceNote: Derived: sample at 69.5 m (FDR Table 4.63) minus FDR Fig. 4.64 image distances (H mirror centre 0.12 m, V mirror centre 0.4 m upstream of focus) → mirror centres ~69.1–69.4 m. FDR Table 4.63 lists the Atomic KB at 68.1 m; FDR text '69 m'; PDR 69 m. Note: the table's 68.1 m coincides with the ray-trace KB2V centre (~68.0–68.15 m, Fig. 4.64, where the implied focus is ~68.4 m), so Table 4.63 appears to mix the ray-trace frame (KB2) with the drawing frame (instrument 69.5 m).
components.text: The second half of the zoom lens, just in front of the sample: a 400 mm mirror that focuses vertically and a 140 mm mirror that focuses horizontally, leaving about 50 mm of working space before the focus. The size of the spot depends on how much of their length is lit, which the first pair sets: fully lit, they converge the beam steeply enough for a spot of about 50 nm, as small as diffraction allows; lit over a short length, the spot grows to about 2 µm, always at the same focal point. Matching the spot to each crystal puts nearly all of the coherent light on it. These are design values: the only published prototype, a one-direction test at 1-BM, reached just 3.2–10.5 µm, limited by mirror shape errors.

specs.1-BM prototype (2020): 1-D, 3.2–10.5 µm FWHM, limited by 4.6 nm rms figure error

components.name: Sample-positioning diffractometer (34ID-BI-3)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63 ('Atomic Endstation Instrument'); FDR Fig. 4.58 instrument footprint ~68.8–70.5 m (approx); PDR 69.05 m.
components.text: The 2017 design concept calls for a massive granite platform carrying the final mirrors and the sample stages, mechanically separate from the detector arm, as at the ID01 beamline of the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility (ESRF). It must turn a crystal to the exact angle at which it reflects and keep it inside a beam as narrow as 50 nm, steady to tens of nanometres over an hour-long scan. The 2019 final design lists separate sample- and detector-positioning diffractometers, and as-built details are not published; the APS Beamline Directory describes a five-circle diffractometer, apparently the instrument inherited from 34-ID-C.

specs.stability: tens of nm over ~1 h (PDR goal)
specs.model (PDR): ESRF ID01-style granite platform, decoupled detector arm

components.name: Sample goniometer and nanopositioning stages
components.distanceNote: At the focus (approx, = instrument position).
components.text: Fine motors and piezo stages rock the crystal through its scan, a fraction of a degree in steps of thousandths of a degree, and centre it in the beam to within nanometres. ATOMIC's as-built stack is not published; the pre-upgrade 34-ID-C stack, which it likely inherits, combined an air-bearing rotation, two tilt circles, coarse translations, a piezo stage with 100 × 100 × 25 µm of travel and a confocal light microscope for finding samples.

components.name: Operando sample environments
components.distanceNote: On the sample stages (approx.). Drawn: a gas-flow heater dome mounted around the sample.
components.text: Small cells let a crystal be imaged while something happens to it: a gas-flow heater from room temperature to 900 °C, a cryo chamber down to about 80 K, a room-temperature liquid-flow cell with a peristaltic pump, a residual-gas analyser and a holder for working coin-cell batteries, charged and discharged by a BioLogic SP300 potentiostat. Shown here: the gas-flow heater dome around the sample.

components.name: Laue orientation detector (Eiger 500K)
components.distanceNote: Close to the sample (at 34-ID-C ~25 mm from focus, on the inboard side facing outboard, movable vertically and inboard/outboard; Zhang et al. 2023); Pateras et al. 2020 used an ASI Timepix GaAs detector 26 mm from the centre of rotation, above and inboard of the beam. Position at 34-ID-F not published: drawn as at 34-ID-C, on the inboard side facing outboard at beam height, sensor face ~28 mm from the sample and centred 30 mm downstream so that it catches forward-scattered Laue spots and clears KB2 (approx.).
components.text: A camera parked a few centimetres from the sample, used only to find the crystal's orientation. When the pink beam, many energies at once, hits the crystal, each set of atomic planes reflects the wavelength that suits its angle, and the camera records a starburst of Laue spots that reveals exactly how the crystal is turned, so the team knows where to find each reflection for coherent imaging. It is an Eiger 500K with 1024 × 512 pixels of 75 µm; at 34-ID-C it sat about 25 mm from the sample.

components.name: Fluorescence detector
components.distanceNote: Near the sample (approx.). Drawn on the outboard side at 90° to the beam in the horizontal plane, where elastic scattering of the horizontally polarized beam is weakest (illustrative position).
components.text: A detector that sorts the X-rays the sample gives off by energy; each element emits its own characteristic energies, so the spectrum confirms what the crystal is made of. It is drawn looking at the sample from the side, in the horizontal plane at 90° to the beam, where scattering of the horizontally polarized beam is weakest. At 34-ID-C this was a silicon drift detector (Vortex EX-60).

components.name: Detector-positioning diffractometer (detector arm)
components.distanceNote: Pivot at the sample (69.5 m); arm ~4.5 m (PDR Fig. 6.7 label '4500'); FDR Fig. 4.58 draws the arm in plan view at ~35° toward the outboard side with a floor arc of radius ~4.1–4.3 m spanning ~8–67° (approx.). Model: boom 4.4 m, posed at δ = 30° (horizontal, outboard) and γ = 16.8° (vertical), i.e. 2θ = 34.0° (Au 111 at 9 keV); the as-built arm geometry is not published.
components.text: A motorised arm more than 4 m long that swings around the sample and lifts the camera to wherever the chosen reflection goes, at distances up to about 5 m. Distance matters: a larger crystal makes finer speckle, so the camera must move farther away for each speckle to span several pixels, and 5 m suffices for crystals up to 1.5–2 µm, the largest single-view Bragg coherent imaging handles. The beam is polarized horizontally, so high-angle reflections are far brighter when scattered upward; the old 34-ID-C arm could rise to 150° but swing only 45° sideways. The new arm's as-built geometry is not published.

components.name: Evacuated flight tube
components.distanceNote: Between sample and BCDI detector along the diffracted beam (used at 34-ID-C). Model: tube from 0.35 m to 2.85 m along the diffracted ray (2θ = 34°); 70.8 m is the along-beam position of its midpoint (illustrative; presence and length on the ATOMIC arm not published).
components.text: An evacuated pipe between sample and camera. Air would scatter and absorb some of the X-rays, adding a background haze and weakening the faint outer speckles; in vacuum they arrive cleanly. 34-ID-C used one for sample–detector distances of about 1 m; whether ATOMIC's arm carries one, and how long, is not published.

components.name: BCDI photon-counting area detector
components.distanceNote: PDR Table 6.5 'DET 72–75 m'; in practice ~0.1–5 m from the sample at angle 2θ_B off the direct beam (PDR; Zhang et al. 2023). Model: 3.0 m from the sample at 2θ = 34.0° (δ 30° outboard, γ 16.8° up), i.e. ~72.0 m along the beam, 1.45 m outboard and 0.87 m above the beam.
components.text: A photon-counting camera: each pixel counts individual X-rays, so even faint outer speckles register. While the crystal is rocked, it records the 3D speckle pattern of one reflection frame by frame. The APS directory lists a Timepix-based detector with 512 × 512 pixels of 55 µm; detector purchases were cut from the upgrade project. Count rate is the bottleneck: the central speckle of a Bragg peak can saturate a pixel, and in the design report's worst case, the full 50 nm beam passing straight through onto a detector 0.2 m away, each pixel would receive about 7 × 10¹⁰ photons per second, against a linear limit near 3 × 10⁶ for Eiger-class pixels.

specs.type: 'TimePix2 512 × 512 55 µm pixel' (directory; vendor not stated; 34-ID-C used ASI Quad Timepix GaAs)
specs.distance needed (PDR, 12 keV, 75 µm pixe: 0.11 m for 50 nm, 3.4 m for 1.5 µm crystals

components.name: Pink beam stop (inboard, 34ID-BS-2)
components.distanceNote: FDR Table 4.63.
components.text: The end of the line, 78.7 m from the source: a heavy block that absorbs whatever beam passes the sample. It keeps X-rays from leaving ATOMIC's shielded hutch, 34-ID-F, which ends about a metre further on.

enclosures.name: 34-ID-A
enclosures.role: First optics enclosure (white beam), shared by ATOMIC and 3DMN
enclosures.notes: Boundaries read from the FDR Fig. 4.58 scale (± ~0.3 m); downstream wall ~35.9–36.0 m (shielded transport ST-1 starts at 36.0 m, FDR Table 4.63). Contains FE exit table, both CUFE white-beam slits, W/Pb collimators, both flat mirrors (3DMN 29.6 m, ATOMIC 31.3 m), secondary collimators, flag and the pink mask / WB stop (34.0 m). The inboard side is the angled storage-ring shield wall.

enclosures.name: Transport
enclosures.role: No hutch: the shielded white-beam pipe 34ID-ST-1 crosses the experiment floor

enclosures.name: 34-ID-B
enclosures.role: Existing small enclosure with pink-beam photon masks and bremsstrahlung stop
enclosures.notes: Approx. from FDR Fig. 4.58. Photon masks PM-2/PM-3 at 46.9 m, BC-3 at 47.3 m. (In PDR 2017 naming 34-ID-B was the SOE.)

enclosures.name: 34-ID-C
enclosures.role: Optics enclosure for both branches (the former 34-ID-C BCDI experiment station, repurposed)
enclosures.notes: Approx. from FDR Fig. 4.58 (width ~3.5 m, beam ~0.8 m from the inboard wall; rough). ATOMIC BPM 49.7, slits S2 50.3, HDCM 51.0, zoom KB1 ~54 m; 3DMN BPM/slits/HDCM 52.7–53.8 m; both pink shutters at 54.8 m. Downstream wall corrected from 55.3 to ~55.0 m: FDR Table 4.63 puts the shutters (in C) at 54.8 m and the start of the 'shielded pipe through 34-ID-E' at 55.1 m.

enclosures.name: 34-ID-E
enclosures.role: 3DMN experiment station; ATOMIC beam passes through in a shielded pipe
enclosures.notes: ATOMIC shielded transport 55.1–67.5 m. See 3DMN dossier for hutch details.

enclosures.name: 34-ID-F
enclosures.notes: Read from FDR Fig. 4.58 (approx. ± 0.3 m): roughly trapezoidal plan – ~7.5 m wide at the upstream wall (beam ~2.0 m from the straight inboard wall, ~5.5 m from the outboard wall), the outboard wall running diagonally (with a step near 75 m) to meet the beam line near the downstream end (~79.8 m on the Fig. 4.58 scale bar), where the hutch is only ~2 m wide (inboard wall to the corner on the beam axis). Diffractometer ~69.5–69.7 m; detector arm swings toward the outboard (wide) side; pink beam stop 78.7 m. PDR (2017) elevation shows this hutch with a higher roof (~3.5 m vs ~2.6 m for the upstream hutches, approx., assuming the APS standard ~1.4 m beam height) to give the detector arm vertical travel. In the PDR this hutch was called '34-ID-E'.

instruments.name: ATOMIC coherent-imaging endstation (FDR design)
instruments.text: The heart of ATOMIC, in the new hutch 34-ID-F. A sample-positioning diffractometer holds a single crystal in the zoomable spot, 50 nm to 2 µm, and turns it to the angle at which it reflects, while a separate detector-positioning diffractometer carries the camera up to about 5 m from the sample to record the speckle. The 2019 Final Design Report adds a beam pre-conditioning platform and two modes, 'Monochromatic CDI' and 'Pink Beam CDI' (coherent diffractive imaging), run independently of 3DMN; the 2017 concept added in situ Laue orientation and a goniometer steady to tens of nanometres over an hour. As-built hardware is not published as of October 2026. The APS Beamline Directory also offers a scanning electron microscope for characterizing samples.
detectors: Other detectors from the APS detector pool (directory)
sampleEnvironments: Room-temperature liquid-flow cell with peristaltic pump

instruments.name: 34-ID-C BCDI instrument (pre-upgrade heritage, operated until the 2023 APS-U dark period)
instruments.text: The station where 3D strain imaging inside a nanocrystal was first demonstrated, in 2006. It ran until the upgrade's 2023 dark period, and its hutch now holds ATOMIC's monochromator and first zoom mirrors. Bendable Kirkpatrick–Baez (KB) mirrors focused its beam to about 0.5 × 0.7 µm, a monochromator that could slide aside allowed pink-beam Laue orientation, and a detector arm placed cameras 0.5–2.5 m from the sample; its 5 mrad platinum mirror set a practical maximum of about 17 keV. Its know-how, software and probably some hardware moved to ATOMIC: the Beamline Directory's 34-ID-F entry (five-circle diffractometer, 70 mm working distance, ~300 nm spot) appears to describe this setup.

geometryNotes:
The beamlines form a canted pair in the sector-34 straight: ATOMIC is the downstream undulator (revolver U21/U25) and the inboard beam, 1.0 mrad from the 3DMN U28 beam (upstream, outboard) (FDR). This reverses the pre-upgrade assignment, when the coherent-imaging station 34-ID-C took the outboard beam and deflected it a further 10 mrad outboard (34-ID wiki, 2013).

All hutches sit on the existing experiment floor within the sector footprint (no long-beamline building). Order along the beam (FDR naming): 34-ID-A FOE ~24.4–36.0 m → shielded transport 36.0–42.5 m → 34-ID-B ~42.3–47.8 m → 34-ID-C ~47.8–55.0 m (optics, the former BCDI station) → 34-ID-E 55.0–67.5 m (3DMN; ATOMIC in a shielded pipe ~0.4 m inboard of the 3DMN beam, approx.) → 34-ID-F 67.5–~79.8 m (the new ATOMIC hutch). Boundaries were re-measured on the FDR Fig. 4.58 scale bar (~25 px/m) and harmonized with the 3DMN dossier; the C/E wall is constrained to ~55.0 m by the shutters (54.8 m) and the start of the shielded pipe (55.1 m).

Naming changed between the PDR (2017: SOE '34-ID-B', 3DMN '34-ID-D', ATOMIC '34-ID-E') and the FDR (2019: C = optics, E = 3DMN, F = ATOMIC).

Deflections: the ATOMIC flat mirror (31.3 m) reflects horizontally at 3.0 mrad grazing (6 mrad deflection) toward the ring (inboard), as drawn in the FDR Fig. 4.59 schematic and stated in the PDR (one mirror outboard for 3DMN, one inboard for ATOMIC; ~11 mrad between the pink beams at the PDR's 2.5 mrad, ~13 mrad at 3.0 mrad, derived), consistent with the ~0.4 m beam separation seen in 34-ID-E in Fig. 4.58. The HDCM deflects horizontally with only ~1.1 mm lateral offset (no vertical offset), so the mono beam is shifted sideways by ~1 mm, not raised.

The zoom KB pairs deflect in both planes by ~6 mrad each (3 mrad grazing; up to 10 mrad at 5 mrad incidence), so the beam axis at the sample is tilted slightly (sense not documented).

Beam height: APS standard ~1.4 m above the floor (consistent with the PDR elevation; approx.).

In 34-ID-F (FDR Fig. 4.58, approx.): the beam runs ~2 m from the straight inboard wall; the hutch is ~7.5 m wide at its upstream wall and narrows along a diagonal outboard wall (with a step near ~74.8 m) to ~2 m at ~79.8 m; diffractometer ~69.5–69.7 m; a ~4.5 m detector arm (PDR label '4500'; the FDR Fig. 4.58 arc has a radius of ~4.2–4.4 m) is drawn in plan view sweeping toward the wide outboard side (a plan view cannot show vertical travel); the PDR elevation shows a taller roof here (~3.5 m) than over the upstream hutches (~2.6 m), for vertical detector travel; pink beam stop at 78.7 m.

Distance inconsistencies: KB1 at 52.0 m (FDR table) vs 54 m (FDR text, FDR/PDR drawings) vs 52.7–53.2 m (FDR ray-trace frame); KB2 at 68.1 m (table) vs ~69.1–69.4 m implied by 0.12/0.4 m image distances and a 69.5 m sample. The ray-trace frame appears ~1.1 m shorter (likely measured from the downstream undulator, not the straight centre). This exhibit uses the drawing frame: KB1 ~54 m, KB2 immediately upstream of a 69.5 m sample, working distance ~50 mm.

Polarization: the undulator beam is linearly polarized in the horizontal plane. Grazing-incidence mirrors are essentially polarization-insensitive; the horizontally deflecting Si(111) DCM passes π-polarization, so its bandwidth and throughput scale as |cos 2θ_{B}| (~0.72 at 5.3 keV, ~0.92 at 10 keV, derived).

For scattering from the sample in the horizontal plane the kinematic intensity factor is cos²(2θ) (0.69 for Au 111 at 9 keV, ~0.25–0.02 at 2θ = 60–80°), which is why the heritage 34-ID-C arm reached high angles mainly vertically (γ up to 150° vs δ up to 45° horizontally).

interactiveIdeas.title: Strain you can see: from speckle to 3D displacement
interactiveIdeas.concept: Visitors deform a cartoon nanocrystal (squeeze a corner, insert a dislocation, adsorb molecules on a facet). Beside it, a live 2D/3D Bragg-peak speckle pattern updates; a perfect crystal gives a symmetric pattern, strain makes it lopsided. A 'reconstruct' button runs a few hundred ER/HIO iterations in the browser and colours the recovered crystal by phase = displacement along G.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: BCDI images shape (amplitude) and atomic displacement (phase) at once; symmetric peaks mean no strain; it is the asymmetry that encodes strain.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: I(q) = |FT{ρ(r) exp(i G·u(r))}|² around q = G; phase φ = G·u, so for Au(111) (d = 2.355 Å) 1 rad = d/2π = 0.375 Å displacement (wraps every 2.355 Å); strain ε_zz = (1/|G|) dφ/dz. Bragg angle λ = 2 d sin(θ): Au(111) at 9 keV → 2θ = 34.0°. Oversampling ≥ 2 per dimension (fringe spacing λ D / s; e.g. 300 nm crystal, 9 keV, 1.1 m → ~505 µm = ~9 pixels of 55 µm). Phase retrieval has trivial ambiguities (global phase, twin/conjugate inversion, translation). A rocking scan of ~0.3-1° samples the third dimension. Real BCDI resolution today ~10-30 nm; do not show atoms unless in the 'future' mode.

interactiveIdeas.title: A zoom lens made of mirrors
interactiveIdeas.concept: A side-view of the 15-m-long two-stage KB system. A slider bends KB1 so its intermediate focus slides from just after KB1 to just before KB2; the beam footprint on KB2, the numerical aperture and the final spot (50 nm to 2 µm) update live, together with flux and a 'sample size' that the spot should match.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Zoom optics change the size of a focused coherent beam without moving the focus; small spots need a large illuminated aperture on the last mirror; matching spot to sample wastes no coherent photons.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Geometry from FDR Fig. 4.64: KB1 350 mm mirrors at p1 ~53 m; KB1→KB2 ~15 m; KB2 H 140 mm with q2 = 0.12 m (50 mm working distance), V 400 mm with q2 = 0.4 m; all at 3 mrad grazing (footprint = beam size / θ, so 350 mm accepts ~1 mm). Coherent illumination → spot is diffraction-limited: FWHM ~0.44 λ/NA for a uniformly filled 1D aperture, with NA ~ (illuminated length × θ)/(2 q2); 50 nm at 8.7 keV needs NA ~1.25 mrad (derived), within reach of KB2H (140 mm × 3 mrad / (2 × 0.12 m) = 1.75 mrad max) and KB2V (400 mm × 3 mrad / (2 × 0.4 m) = 1.5 mrad max); PDR: ~2.3 × 2.5 mrad divergence for 50 nm, ~65 × 70 µrad for 1.5 µm. Geometric source image M = (q1/p1)(q2/p2) is smaller than the diffraction limit at 50 nm, so do not model the small end as source demagnification. Figure error must be <1 nm rms. Flux values: 3.1 × 10¹² (50 nm) vs 4.6 × 10¹² ph/s/0.1%BW (2 µm) at 8.7 keV.

interactiveIdeas.title: Flashlight vs laser: coherence before and after the upgrade
interactiveIdeas.concept: Two electron-beam cross-sections (old 280 × 10 µm rms vs new 14.7 × 3.2 µm) launch wavefronts down a 50 m beamline; a double-slit or nanocrystal at the end shows fringe visibility. Visitors close the S1/S2 slits to filter coherence and watch flux drop vs visibility rise.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Only the coherent part of the beam makes sharp speckle; APS-U makes the beam ~100× more coherent at ~10 keV so the slits throw away far fewer photons.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Total photon source Σ = √(σe² + σr²), Σ' = √(σe'² + σr'²), σr = √(2 λ L)/4π, σr' = √(λ/2L), L = 2.1 m; coherent fraction per plane = (λ/4π)/(Σ Σ'): ~0.11 (H) × 0.48 (V) at 10 keV for APS-U brightness mode vs ~0.003 × 0.16 before (derived from FDR Table 1.1). Transverse coherence length at distance z ~ λ z/(2 π Σ) (one common convention; ~70 µm H at 50 m, 10 keV, APS-U vs ~3.5 µm before). Longitudinal coherence λ²/(2 Δλ) ~0.5 µm at 10 keV for Si(111) (PDR) - path differences across the crystal must stay below this. Coherent flux at 20 keV up ~520× (FDR Table 1.1).

interactiveIdeas.title: The photon budget for seeing atoms
interactiveIdeas.concept: A resolution slider from 30 nm to 0.2 nm shows how far out in reciprocal space the detector must see, how fast the speckle intensity falls, and the dose and beam time needed - with the old APS, APS-U, and a 'radiation damage / heating' warning light.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Resolution is limited by how many photons you can collect at high scattering angles, not by lenses; atomic resolution is a photon (and detector, and sample-survival) problem that APS-U makes approachable.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Half-period resolution ~π/q_max (2π/q_max is the smallest lattice period sampled; e.g. q_max = 1.26 Å⁻¹ → ~2.5 Å half-period); for a compact object the speckle envelope falls ~q⁻⁴ (Porod), so dose rises steeply (roughly as resolution⁻⁴ for fixed signal per voxel); Dietze & Shpyrko: ~10¹⁸ ph/µm² for atomic resolution of a 20 nm Au crystal, ~10¹⁷ for amorphous Au. At 3.1 × 10¹² ph/s in a 50 × 50 nm² spot (1.2 × 10¹⁵ ph/s/µm²) 10¹⁸ ph/µm² takes ~800 s (derived; PDR estimate ~1000 s). Focused power ~8 mW in 50 × 50 nm² at 10 keV (PDR) - sample heating and damage matter. Detector: the unattenuated transmitted 50 nm beam on 75 µm pixels at 0.2 m would be ~7 × 10¹⁰ ph/s/pixel vs ~3 × 10⁶ linear limit (PDR worst case; Bragg-peak speckles are much weaker).

interactiveIdeas.title: Find the crystal: Laue then Bragg
interactiveIdeas.concept: A game: a random sub-micron grain sits on a substrate. Visitors first flash the pink beam to get a Laue starburst on the near detector, click to index it, then swing the detector arm and rock the sample to land the coherent reflection on the far detector, finally choosing three reflections to build the full strain tensor.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Why the beamline keeps a pink-beam bypass and a near-sample Laue detector; how orientation finding turns a needle-in-a-haystack search into a few clicks; why three non-coplanar reflections give the full strain tensor.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Pink-beam bandwidth at 34-ID-C ~5-20 keV: every reciprocal-lattice point between the Ewald spheres for E_min and E_max diffracts at once; orientation accuracy ~0.01° possible with known energy calibration; mono beam then aligned with heated second DCM crystal so pink and mono beams share a focus. Each reflection gives u·G_hkl; three non-coplanar G give u(r) and the 6-component strain tensor. Detector 2θ for Au 333/400 at 12 keV is ~60-80° (PDR); horizontal-plane scattering suffers the cos²(2θ) polarization factor in intensity (horizontally polarized beam), so high-angle reflections are better reached by vertical detector motion (34-ID-C γ to 150°).

funFacts: The first 3D image of the strain field inside a single nanocrystal, a lead crystal, was made at 34-ID-C, ATOMIC's predecessor, and published in Nature in 2006.

The name is aspirational: the beamline's designer describes 'Atomic' as meant to be inspirational, asking whether coherent X-ray imaging can finally reach wavelength-limited (atomic) resolution. It began as APS-U white paper WP28 in January 2016.

In the 2019 design, the old coherent-imaging hutch 34-ID-C becomes an optics hutch holding ATOMIC's monochromator and the first half of its zoom lens, while the new experiment hutch 34-ID-F was built at the end of the line.
ATOMIC and its twin 3DMN start from the same roughly 5 m straight section; their beams leave it just 1 milliradian apart, about 2.5 cm apart after 25 m.
ATOMIC's undulator is a 'revolver': two magnet arrays (21 and 25 mm periods) on a strongback that rotates 90° to swap them.

The zoom mirrors must keep their shape errors below 1 nm rms, a few atoms high, along mirrors up to 40 cm long, even while being bent. (For comparison, the 2017 design report, discussing an ultra-stable goniometer, notes that the Hubble Space Telescope mirror's figure error is about 30 nm.)

If the full, unattenuated 50 nm beam passed straight through a sample onto a detector 20 cm away, each 75 µm pixel would receive about 7 × 10¹⁰ photons per second, roughly 20,000 times what an Eiger-class pixel can count linearly (the design report's worst case).
ATOMIC is expected to produce 250–300 terabytes of data a year, about 400 times more than its predecessor 34-ID-C (~0.65 TB a year).
Focused into 50 × 50 nm², the beam carries about 8 milliwatts (a design estimate at 10 keV), so keeping the sample from heating up becomes part of the experiment design.

Bragg coherent imaging maps of displacement are sensitive to shifts of a small fraction of an atomic spacing: a 2017 Science study of a heated gold film reached 10 nm spatial and sub-ångström displacement resolution.
